text: QR, SVD and least squares Least squares, low-rank approximation and conditioning call for different matrix decompositions. QR reduces a problem to orthogonal transformations and a triangular solve; SVD exposes singular values and resolvable directions. Problem and representative equations For a real m×n matrix with m≥n, thin QR has QᵀQ=I and upper triangular R. Full column rank gives the least-squares solve Rx=Qᵀb. SVD has nonnegative singular values σᵢ. Truncating small σᵢ in a pseudoinverse regularizes the problem and can change the solution being sought. Algorithm Householder QR eliminates subdiagonal entries with reflections and generally maintains orthogonality better than classical Gram–Schmidt. Consider column pivoting or SVD for rank diagnosis. Classical SVD algorithms reduce to bidiagonal form using orthogonal transformations rather than explicitly forming normal equations. Conditions and pitfalls For full column rank, κ₂(AᵀA)=κ₂(A)². A small residual can coexist with uncertain coefficients under ill-conditioning or noise. Choose a numerical-rank threshold relative to scale, rounding and measurement uncertainty, and consider column scaling when variables have different units. Distinguish residual/backward error from forward errors in coefficients or singular values. At large condition numbers, small changes to the input or right-hand side can cause large coefficient changes. Numerical rank depends on a singular-value threshold and arithmetic precision; a truncated least-squares solution need not solve the original problem exactly. General least-squares sensitivity also depends on the angle between the right-hand side and the column space, not only on condition number. Published relative-accuracy results for one-sided Jacobi SVD depend on stopping rules and componentwise conditioning. Agreement for small singular values in these small matrices is not a universal relative-accuracy guarantee for arbitrary ill-conditioned matrices.
